 Live .  4,345 viewing 4345 viewing Live page Updated 1 minute ago Brazil's left-wing President Lula elected for fourth term, beating Flávio Bolsonaro in surprise result
 Summary
 Brazil's left-wing President Lula wins a fourth term in office, defeating his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro
 The 80-year-old, who took just under 52% of the vote , tells cheering supporters in São Paulo that Brazilians had voted to "guarantee democracy"
 Bolsonaro - who won the first round - says the result is "inexplicable" and calls for it to be annulled - our Latin America editor explains what's happening 
 His father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is currently under house arrest for plotting a coup after losing the last election
 This election was bitterly fought - and it bucks a wider regional trend towards right-wing leaders, our Latin America editor writes 
 Follow live coverage from BBC Brasil in Portuguese

 Live Reporting
 Edited by Dulcie Lee and James Chater, with reporting from Ione Wells in Brasília and the BBC's Brasil service
 A surprising and historic election win for Lula published at 03:43 GMT 03:43 GMT 
 Caio Quero 
BBC News Brasil editor 
 Image source, Reuters President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was elected to a fourth term after defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the runoff of Brazil’s presidential election. 
 With 98.87% of ballot boxes counted, Brazil’s electoral court (TSE) declared Lula mathematically elected. The incumbent president secured 51.76% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.24%, a wider margin than his victory over Flávio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, in 2022.
 The result came as a surprise, marking the first time since Brazil's return to democracy that a candidate who lost the first round managed to overturn the result and win the presidency. 
 It followed a massive campaign by Lula’s supporters on social media and street demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands of people to Brazil’s main cities, including Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo.
 Election day was also marked by high voter turnout, with the largest drop in abstention between the first and second rounds of a presidential election in democratic elections since 1989. 
 The day, however, was marred by controversy, with Lula’s campaign alleging voter suppression after a shortage of buses left voters struggling to reach polling stations in several cities, including São Paulo and Salvador, in north-eastern Brazil. 
 Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign also called for an extension of voting hours because of adverse weather conditions in southern Brazil. The Supreme Court eventually extended voting by two hours.
 Jair Bolsonaro is currently under arrest after being convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup d’état after losing the 2022 elections against Lula.
 Lula becomes the first president in Brazilian history to win a fourth term and will remain in office until 2030.

 More than 4 million votes between Lula and Bolsonaro published at 03:24 GMT 03:24 GMT 
 Ione Wells 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Image source, Reuters From the official count data we are seeing, this was close - but not as close as the first round. 
 There were more than 4 million votes between President Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, or about 3 points. That’s more than the 2 points that Bolsonaro won the first round with. 
 It’s too early to say what made this difference - but we do know that President Lula’s campaign really gained momentum in the last few weeks and had an energy to it that we didn’t see in the first round. 
 Their major strategy was also to try boost the voter turnout, after 33 million people didn’t vote in round one.

 Why is Bolsonaro calling for the result to be annulled - and what happens next? published at 03:08 GMT 03:08 GMT 
 Vanessa Buschschlüter 
Latin America and Caribbean editor 
 Image source, Getty Images Flávio Bolsonaro had been expecting a victory tonight. His reaction to his election loss has been to question the result.
 He said it was "impossible to recognise" even though with all of the results now in, he is trailing with 48.21% compared to Lula's 51.79%.
 He is calling for an annulment of the election, and the reason he is giving is that "the rules of the game were changed".
 What he is referring to is the decision by the Supreme Court to extend voting by two hours. 
 While it was an unusual decision, it was one which had been formally requested by both Lula and Bolsonaro's campaign teams. 
 Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of busses.
 Bolsonaro's team cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.
 In his first public appearance, Bolsonaro said he would get his campaign's legal team to request the annulment.
 No doubt the legal team is now busy hammering out the arguments it will put before the court to back up its claim.

 Bolsonaro visibly angry as he decried election result published at 02:54 GMT 02:54 GMT 
 Branca Lessa de Sa 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Media caption, Flávio Bolsonaro calls for elections to be annulled
 Flávio Bolsonaro was visibly angry as he delivered comments outside of the home in Brasília a little earlier.
 He said that a lot would need to be "cleared up" before this "sacanagem" - a Brazilian term meaning dirty trick - could be accepted.
 Pablo Marçal, an influencer and former mayoral candidate who has been coordinating a social media campaign in support of Bolsonaro, also spoke after leaving the house in Brasilia.
 He said the decision by Brazil’s Supreme Court to extend voting hours was a "tragedy".
 As a reminder, both sides asked for extensions to voting hours for different reasons - read more here .
 We'll bring you more details to explain the fallout - and what could happen next - shortly.

 Brazil papers call Lula's win 'historic' published at 02:41 GMT 02:41 GMT 
 Pascal Fletcher 
Latin American Specialist, BBC Monitoring 
 Many media outlets in Brazil have been describing the result as a "historic turnaround" for Lula.
 Lula's victory represented "a historic turnaround in the hardest-fought election race in [Brazil's] history," Brasilia-based daily Correio Braziliense wrote.
 Brazilian news magazine Veja noted that Lula had managed to achieve a number of firsts in his country's electoral history: he becomes the first Brazilian politician to win the presidency four times, and also the first candidate to win a run-off vote after finishing second in the earlier round of voting. 
 Daily O Estado de S. Paulo and other outlets reported on Lula's jubilant supporters celebrating in the central Avenida Paulista of Brazil's largest city, São Paulo.

 'Long live democracy!': Regional leaders congratulate Lula published at 02:09 GMT 02:09 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said the people of Brazil had "won"
 Leaders from across Latin America are sending congratulations to Lula.
 Paraguay President Santiago Peña posted on X: "I salute the Brazilian people for this great democratic journey".
 Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on social media: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
 Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz said:"Bolivia and Brazil are neighbouring and brother countries, united by a shared history and common challenges. We will continue working together to strengthen our relationship and generate more opportunities for ​our nations."
 Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel called it an "historic victory" which "ensures the continuity of ​the ⁠path of peace, sovereignty, and social justice embarked upon by the Brazilian people under your leadership".
 Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi called Lula a "friend" and said he had "congratulated him ​on the victory and on the democratic celebration that ​an electoral process represents".
 Panama President José Raúl Mulino said: "I ⁠congratulate ​the Brazilian people for this democratic ​day and especially President Lula for the victory!"

 Tears and heartbreak among Bolsonaro supporters published at 02:00 GMT 02:00 GMT 
 Earlier, we brought you photos of jubilant Lula supporters .
 However, it's a different story for supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro who were visibly upset at the outcome.
 The son of the former president, who is currently under house arrest, has so far refused to recognise Lula's victory .

 Bolsonaro refuses to recognise Lula's victory and calls for result to be annulled published at 01:49 GMT 01:49 GMT Breaking 
 Ione Wells 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Image source, Getty Images Flávio Bolsonaro was expecting to give a victory speech tonight here in Brasília after winning the first round. 
 Instead, he just said that what happened was “impossible” and “inexplicable” and said the result should be annulled. 
 His supporters chanted his name as he left. This lack of recognition of the result could sow a lot of distrust among his supporters. 
 With his comments tonight, he follows in his father Jair Bolsonaro’s footsteps - he too refused to recognise his election loss in 2022.

 Bolsonaro team was set for a victory speech published at 01:43 GMT 01:43 GMT 
 Ione Wells 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Huge crowds of press are gathered at the house here in Brasília where Flavio Bolsonaro was watching the result. 
 The scene was set for a victory party and speech, with a big screen and supporters of his inside. 
 When it was clear which way the wind was blowing, some of those supporters left early looking despondent and in some cases visibly annoyed. 
 We are waiting for Flavio Bolsonaro to speak - the big question is whether or not he will accept this result.

 This country will not accept being anyone's back yard - Lula published at 01:42 GMT 01:42 GMT 
 Vanessa Buschschlüter 
Latin America and Caribbean editor 
 In his victory speech, Lula again stresses that Brazil will "not accept being anyone's backyard".
 This has been one of phrases he has repeated time and time again in his campaign.
 It refers to the term "America's backyard" - a pithy way to describe the idea in US policy that Latin America should be under the sphere of influence of the United States.
 That idea is one that President Donald Trump has enshrined in what he himself has called "Donroe Doctrine" but which has raised hackles in Latin America.
 President Lula's defence of Brazil's sovereignty is one of the things which pollsters think won him votes, with voters rejecting what they saw as US interference.

 This election is a 'loss for negativity and lies' - Lula published at 01:26 GMT 01:26 GMT 
 Lula thanks those who coordinated his campaign, as well as the "generosity of Brazilian people", including young people, who he says "went to the streets to defend Brazilian democracy".
 People voted because we could convince them that the vote was important for the sovereignty of our country, he tells the crowds.
 He says this election was a "loss for negativity, lies".

 'Our throats are very tired,' a hoarse Lula tells thrilled crowds published at 01:21 GMT 01:21 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images "Our throats are very tired," Lula begins, with a hoarse voice.
 He almost immediately hands over to his Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, who he says he wants to speak first.
 "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy," Alckmin tells Lula.

 Joao Fellet 
BBC Brasil, reporting from São Paulo 
 Image source, Getty Images Lula's supporters are celebrating intensely, many of them in tears.
 Many didn't believe this victory would be possible. People are setting fireworks and singing.
 São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista turned into a carnival block on a Sunday night.

 Ione Wells 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Outside the house where Flávio Bolsonaro was watching the result, some of his supporters are leaving - some looking visibly angry and despondent.
 The scene here had been set for a victory party.

 Lula proves he is the comeback kid, again published at 00:36 GMT 00:36 GMT 
 Vanessa Buschschlüter 
Latin America and Caribbean editor 
 Image source, Getty Images When President Lula lost to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of this election, many analysts said he had reached the end of the political road. 
 They pointed to the fact that no candidate had ever been able to recover from a first-round loss to go on to win in the run-off. They also insisted that opinion polls often underestimated the support for right-wing candidates.
 Lula himself, though, had seemed confident, telling his supporters to have faith and rally in his support. 
 The veteran leader has of course been written off before. In 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sent to jail for more than 18 months.
 Those convictions were annulled in 2021 , leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro.
 Now he has beaten Jair Bolsonaro's son, showing once more that he is a formidable political opponent, even at 80 years of age.

 A huge upset for Bolsonaro published at 00:28 GMT 00:28 GMT 
 Ione Wells 
Reporting from Brasília 
 Brazil’s President Lula da Silva has just been elected for a fourth term. 
 This is a huge upset for the Flávio Bolsonaro campaign.
No candidate since democracy was restored in 1988 has won the second round after not winning the first round of voting. 
 Voting was delayed for two hours after both campaigns complained about disruptions to voting, caused by the public transport system in some cities and bad weather. 
 Despite this, Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign had already raised doubts about the process before the result was announced.
